title: Starting with yourself
hookLine: the old manuals begin metta with oneself, the easiest proof that everyone wants to be happy
last: METTA — MAY YOU BE AT EASE.

lines: I HOPE YOU HAVE A GOOD DAY.
I HOPE I HAVE A GOOD DAY.
cards: Quick test. Say to a friend: I hope you have a good day. Easy.
Now say it to yourself, out loud: I hope I have a good day. For a lot of people, that second one feels strange. Embarrassing, even.
Selfish. As if kindness only goes outward. So here's a surprise from the old Buddhist manuals.
When they teach metta step by step, the very first person they tell you to wish well is not your mother, not a teacher, not the world. It's you.

teach.h: THE PATH OF PURIFICATION, CHAPTER NINE.
teach.b: The manual is the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, written by the monk Buddhaghosa in Sri Lanka around the fifth century.
Its ninth chapter, on loving-kindness, says to begin by wishing yourself well: may I be happy, may I be free from suffering. Why start there? Not because you're the most important person in the room.
Almost the opposite. When you wish yourself well, you notice something plain: I want to be happy. I don't want to suffer.
Use that as your example, the manual says. Everyone else wants exactly the same thing, just as much.
Your own wish is the easiest proof. The manual backs this up with a teaching from the Pali texts.
King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika, the story goes, admit to each other that nobody is dearer to them than themselves. The Buddha doesn't scold them.

He answers with a verse, in substance: search every direction, and you won't find anyone dearer to a person than their own self; since each one holds themselves that dear, whoever loves themselves should harm no one.
So starting with yourself isn't the selfish shortcut. It's the doorway. Metta for yourself alone isn't the goal, the manual says; it's where you learn what the wish feels like, so you can hand it on.
And on a hard day, the voice in your head that says you don't deserve kindness is exactly the voice this practice answers.

how: In many Buddhist metta practices, especially those following the Visuddhimagga, practitioners begin by wishing themselves well before extending the wish to others.

games.q: the king and queen admit nobody is dearer to them than themselves. what does the Buddha do?
o: say that's why no one should harm others.
tell them to love themselves less.
games.why: he answers with a verse: everyone holds themselves that dear, so whoever loves themselves should harm no one.

practice: Rest your hands somewhere comfortable, maybe one over your heart, and offer the phrases to yourself slowly, with space between: may I be safe, may I be happy, may I be healthy, may I live with ease.
If it feels awkward, that's normal; let the awkwardness be there too. If it helps, picture yourself as a small child and say the words to them.

wordCard.voice: Atta. Oneself: the old manuals begin metta with you, since your own wish to be happy shows you what everyone wants.

orig.note: Pali: oneself; in the verse to Pasenadi, no one is dearer to a person than attā, one's own self.

carryVoice: Your line: you count too. It closes a week that began with the last long Jatakas and the end of the story camp, and ends with metta, step by step. That's day ninety-eight.
